clinicalPearls: The most common autosomal chromosomal disorder and a leading genetic cause of intellectual disability, resulting from an extra copy of chromosome 21.
Most cases are due to meiotic nondisjunction, with incidence rising markedly with advancing maternal age; a minority result from translocation or mosaicism.
Recognisable features include hypotonia, upslanting palpebral fissures, epicanthic folds, a flat nasal bridge, small ears, a single transverse palmar crease, and a sandal gap between the toes.
Congenital heart disease is common, particularly atrioventricular septal defects, so early echocardiography is recommended.
Gastrointestinal anomalies such as duodenal atresia and Hirschsprung disease occur more frequently.
There is increased risk of hypothyroidism, hearing and visual impairment, obstructive sleep apnoea, and atlantoaxial instability, warranting scheduled surveillance.
Children have a higher risk of transient myeloproliferative disorder in the newborn period and of leukaemia in childhood.
Diagnosis is confirmed by karyotype, which also identifies translocations relevant to recurrence risk and family counselling.
Early developmental support and coordinated multidisciplinary care improve developmental and health outcomes.
reference.pathophysiology: The presence of a third copy of chromosome 21 leads to over-expression of the genes it carries, disrupting normal development across multiple organ systems in a dosage-dependent manner. This gene-dosage imbalance affects neurodevelopment, cardiac and gastrointestinal morphogenesis, immune function, and haematopoiesis. Most trisomy 21 arises from failure of chromosomal separation during meiosis (nondisjunction), while translocation and mosaic forms produce the extra genetic material through other mechanisms.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital hypothyroidism (overlapping hypotonia and coarse features)
Zellweger and other syndromes with hypotonia
Other syndromic causes of intellectual disability
additionalInvestigations: Karyotype to confirm trisomy 21 and identify translocation or mosaicism
Echocardiography to detect congenital heart disease
Thyroid function testing at birth and on a scheduled basis
Full blood count to screen for transient myeloproliferative disorder and later leukaemia
Cervical spine assessment when symptoms suggest atlantoaxial instability
redFlags: Signs of significant congenital heart disease or heart failure
Bilious vomiting or abdominal signs suggesting intestinal obstruction
Neurological signs of cervical cord compression from atlantoaxial instability
Persistent pallor, bruising, or abnormal blood counts suggesting leukaemia
reference.prognosis: Life expectancy has improved substantially with modern medical and surgical care and now commonly extends into adulthood; outcomes depend largely on cardiac disease and other complications, and most individuals have mild to moderate intellectual disability with early-onset Alzheimer-type changes in later life.
pitfalls: Assuming a normal heart without echocardiographic screening
Overlooking hypothyroidism, which can mimic or worsen developmental delay
Missing atlantoaxial instability before activities or anaesthesia in symptomatic children
Failing to follow structured health surveillance recommendations
